items.stem: Why does the volume of a real gas at very high pressure exceed the ideal value?
items.answer: The volume of the particles themselves is no longer negligible.
items.markingKey: The volume of the particles themselves is no longer negligible. At high p, particle volume is a significant fraction of the total.

items.stem: Distinguish between a real gas and an ideal gas.
items.answer: An ideal gas has particles of zero volume with no intermolecular forces and obeys pV = nRT exactly; a real gas has particles of finite volume with attractions and deviates, especially at high p and low T.
items.markingKey: An ideal gas has particles of zero volume with no intermolecular forces and obeys pV = nRT exactly; a real gas has particles of finite volume with attractions and deviates, especially at high p and low T. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The ideal gas model assumes that gas particles have no mass." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The model assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces, not zero mass; particle mass determines momentum transfer in collisions.
items.markingKey: The model assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces, not zero mass; particle mass determines momentum transfer in collisions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 1.00 mol of methane at 350 K and 20000 kPa occupies 0.137 dm³. Calculate the volume predicted by the ideal gas equation, the ratio pV/(nRT), and explain the deviation.
items.answer: ideal 0.145 dm³; pV/nRT = 0.939
items.markingKey: V(ideal) = nRT/p = 1.00 × 8.31 × 350/(20000 × 10³) m³ = 0.145 dm³ (M1 A1); pV/nRT = 0.137/0.145 = 0.939 (A1); < 1 because intermolecular attractions (London forces) reduce the pressure/volume (R1).

items.stem: At the same temperature and pressure, which gas shows the greatest deviation from ideal behaviour?
items.answer: ammonia
items.markingKey: D. ammonia: hydrogen bonding. Deviation increases with intermolecular forces and particle size.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The ideal gas model is useful even though no real gas is ideal."
items.answer: The model is valuable within its domain of validity; for high pressure or low temperature, corrected models (e.g. van der Waals) are required – a NOS example of model limitations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: accurate within a few percent for most gases near room conditions; simple equation allows quick calculations; basis of molar volume and gas stoichiometry. Arguments against: fails for high-pressure industrial processes (e.g. Haber process at 20 MPa); cannot predict condensation; polar gases deviate significantly. Supported judgement: The model is valuable within its domain of validity; for high pressure or low temperature, corrected models (e.g. van der Waals) are required – a NOS example of model limitations.

items.stem: Define the term "elastic collision".
items.answer: A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the particles is conserved
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a collision in which the total kinetic energy of the particles is conserved. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A theoretical gas whose particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, move randomly and undergo perfectly elastic collisions, so that it obeys pV = nRT exactly"?
items.answer: ideal gas
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of ideal gas.

items.stem: Which change makes nitrogen gas behave less ideally?
options: increasing the temperature at constant pressure
decreasing the temperature at constant pressure
decreasing the pressure at constant temperature
increasing the volume of the container
items.answer: decreasing the temperature at constant pressure
items.markingKey: B. Lower T → attractions more significant.

items.stem: Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at low temperatures.
items.answer: At low temperature the particles move more slowly, so intermolecular attractions become significant compared with their kinetic energy; collisions with the walls are less forceful and pressure (pV) is lower than predicted.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: At low temperature the particles move more slowly, so intermolecular attractions become significant compared with their kinetic energy; collisions with the walls are less forceful and pressure (pV) is lower than predicted. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Freya writes: "The ideal gas model assumes that gas particles have no mass." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The model assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces, not zero mass; particle mass determines momentum transfer in collisions.
items.markingKey: The model assumes negligible particle volume and no intermolecular forces, not zero mass; particle mass determines momentum transfer in collisions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure.
items.answer: Particles are forced close together, so the volume of the particles is a significant fraction of the container and intermolecular forces become significant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Particles are forced close together, so the volume of the particles is a significant fraction of the container and intermolecular forces become significant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Samples of hydrogen, ammonia, nitrogen and sulfur dioxide are all at 250 K and 5000 kPa. Which gas behaves most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: C. hydrogen: very weak London forces. Deviation from ideal behaviour increases with the strength of intermolecular forces and the size of the particles.

items.stem:
A student released butane gas from a lighter into an inverted measuring cylinder filled with water, collecting 100.0 cm³ of gas. The room temperature was 294 K and atmospheric pressure 99.9 kPa. The vapour pressure of water at 294 K is 2.49 kPa.

mass of lighter before / g ± 0.01 | 19.33
mass of lighter after (dried) / g ± 0.01 | 19.09

(a) Calculate the partial pressure of butane in the cylinder. [1]
(b) Calculate the amount of butane collected. [2]
(c) Determine the experimental molar mass of butane and its percentage error compared with 58.14 g mol⁻¹. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of butane released. [2]
(e) Explain why ignoring the vapour pressure of water would give a lower molar mass (58.7 g mol⁻¹). [1]
items.answer: (a) 97.41 kPa (b) 0.00399 mol (c) 60.2 g mol⁻¹; 3.5 % (d) 8.3 % (e) Using the total pressure overestimates the partial pressure and therefore the amount of butane; M = m/n is then too small.

items.stem: Under which conditions does water vapour behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: high temperature and low pressure
items.markingKey: A. High T: kinetic energy overcomes attractions; low p: particles far apart so their volume is negligible.

items.stem: For a sample of sulfur dioxide at 500 K and 10000 kPa, the measured value of pV/(nRT) is 1.07. Which statement best explains this value?
options: The particles have a lower kinetic energy than predicted.
The attractive forces between the particles are significant.
The gas behaves ideally under these conditions.
The volume of the particles themselves is significant.
items.answer: The volume of the particles themselves is significant.
items.markingKey: D. pV/nRT = 1 for an ideal gas. Greater than 1: the finite particle volume reduces free space, so the real volume exceeds the ideal volume.

items.stem: What are the SI units of pressure and volume in pV = nRT?
items.answer: Pa and m³
items.markingKey: Pa and m³. With R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ use Pa and m³ (or kPa with dm³, which also gives J).

items.stem: Explain why a graph of V against temperature in °C for a gas at constant pressure does not pass through the origin.
items.answer: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature; on the Celsius scale zero is 273 K, so the line extrapolates to zero volume at −273 °C rather than at 0 °C.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature; on the Celsius scale zero is 273 K, so the line extrapolates to zero volume at −273 °C rather than at 0 °C. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between Charles's law and Boyle's law.
items.answer: Boyle's law relates p and V at constant T (inverse proportionality); Charles's law relates V and T at constant p (direct proportionality with T in K).
items.markingKey: Boyle's law relates p and V at constant T (inverse proportionality); Charles's law relates V and T at constant p (direct proportionality with T in K). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A car tyre contains air at 200 kPa and 25 °C. After driving, the temperature of the air is 50 °C. Assuming constant volume, calculate the new pressure.
items.answer: 217 kPa
items.markingKey: p/T constant (M1); p₂ = 200 × 323/298 = 217 kPa (A1).

items.stem: Zara writes: "In pV = nRT, volume can be entered in dm³ with pressure in Pa." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Units must be consistent: Pa with m³ (or kPa with dm³); Pa with dm³ gives an answer 1000 times too large.
items.markingKey: Units must be consistent: Pa with m³ (or kPa with dm³); Pa with dm³ gives an answer 1000 times too large. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A weather balloon is filled with 8.0 m³ of helium at 100 kPa and 15 °C at ground level. It rises to an altitude where the pressure is 20.0 kPa and the temperature is −56 °C. (a) Calculate the amount of helium. (b) Calculate the volume of the balloon at altitude. (c) Explain, with reference to particles, which change (p or T) has the greater effect on the volume.
items.markingKey: (a) n = pV/RT = 334 mol (M1 A1). (b) V₂ = p₁V₁T₂/(T₁p₂) = 30.1 m³ (M1 A1). (c) pressure falls by a factor of 5.0 while T falls by only 1.33; fewer collisions per unit area outside allow expansion – pressure dominates (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant)"?
items.answer: Charles's law
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of Charles's law.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Charles's law"?
options: A graduated syringe used to measure volumes of gas, typically to ±0.5 cm³
For a fixed amount of gas at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature (p/T = constant)
For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant)
A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the particles is conserved
items.answer: For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant)
items.markingKey: C. "Charles's law" is for a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature (V/T = constant).

items.stem: A sealed flask of gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K. What happens to the pressure?
items.answer: It doubles.
items.markingKey: B. p ∝ T at constant V.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Charles's law and Boyle's law.

items.stem: The absolute temperature of a fixed mass of gas is doubled and its pressure is halved. What happens to the volume?
options: It increases by a factor of four.
items.answer: It increases by a factor of four.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "If the temperature of a gas rises from 10 °C to 20 °C at constant pressure, its volume doubles." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Volume ∝ absolute temperature: 283 K → 293 K increases V by only 3.5 %.
items.markingKey: Volume ∝ absolute temperature: 283 K → 293 K increases V by only 3.5 %. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the pressure of a gas increases when its volume is reduced at constant temperature.
items.answer: The same number of particles occupy a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often per unit area; average kinetic energy is unchanged, so pressure increases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The same number of particles occupy a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often per unit area; average kinetic energy is unchanged, so pressure increases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: 83.3 cm³

items.stem: Calculate the volume, in dm³, occupied by 0.514 mol of nitrogen in a bulb at 293 K and 100 kPa.
items.answer: 12.5 dm³

items.answer: 6.37 dm³
items.markingKey: D. V/T constant: V₂ = 5.00 × 373/293 = 6.37 dm³ (T in K).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "pV = nRT is the only gas equation a chemist needs."
items.answer: It is the central equation but must be applied within its ideal limits and with consistent units.

Arguments against: not valid for real gases at high pressure/low temperature; combined gas law (p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂) is more convenient when n is constant. Supported judgement: It is the central equation but must be applied within its ideal limits and with consistent units.

items.stem: A diver at a depth of 40 m (pressure 504 kPa) fills her lungs with 3.0 dm³ of air and then rises to the surface (100 kPa) without exhaling. Assume constant temperature. (a) Calculate the volume the air would occupy at the surface. (b) Explain, using kinetic theory, why the volume increases. (c) Comment on why divers are trained to exhale while ascending.
items.answer: (a) 15.1 dm³
items.markingKey: (a) p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (M1); V₂ = 504 × 3.0/100 = 15.1 dm³ (A1). (b) Lower external pressure; gas particles collide with the walls; volume increases until internal pressure equals external pressure (R1 R1). (c) The air would expand to many times the lung volume, risking lung damage (R1).

(a) Calculate the amount of N₂ required. (b) Calculate the minimum mass of sodium azide, NaN₃, needed. (c) Suggest why the real gas behaviour of N₂ makes little difference here.
items.markingKey: (a) n = pV/RT = 140 × 10³ × 65.0 × 10⁻³/(8.31 × 320) (M1) = 3.42 mol (A1). (b) n(NaN₃) = 2/3 × n(N₂) = 2.28 mol (M1); × 65.02 = 148 g (A1). (c) Moderate pressure and temperature; N₂ is non-polar with weak forces – close to ideal (R1).

items.stem: A 0.200 g sample of a gas occupies 0.112 dm³ at STP. What is its molar mass?

items.stem: In an experiment to determine the molar mass of a gas using M = mRT/(pV), the gas being studied is polar and has significant intermolecular attractions. What is the effect on the calculated molar mass?
options: The effect cannot be predicted from the equation.
items.answer: It will be too high.
items.markingKey: A. Attractions make the real volume smaller than the ideal value, so pV/RT underestimates n and M = m/n is too high.

items.stem: In a gas syringe experiment, the plunger sticks slightly so the volume reading is too small. What is the effect on the calculated molar mass?

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Determining molar mass from gas measurements is less useful today than mass spectrometry."

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Boyle's law".
items.answer: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ideal gas"?
options: A theoretical gas whose particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, move randomly and undergo perfectly elastic collisions, so that it obeys pV = nRT exactly
The constant of proportionality in pV = nRT, 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹
PV = nRT, where p is pressure in Pa, V volume in m³, n amount in mol, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and T temperature in K
For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant)
items.answer: A theoretical gas whose particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, move randomly and undergo perfectly elastic collisions, so that it obeys pV = nRT exactly
items.markingKey: A. "ideal gas" is a theoretical gas whose particles have negligible volume, no intermolecular forces, move randomly and undergo perfectly elastic collisions, so that it obeys pV = nRT exactly.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "gas syringe".
items.answer: A graduated syringe used to measure volumes of gas, typically to ±0.5 cm³
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a graduated syringe used to measure volumes of gas, typically to ±0.5 cm³. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "If the temperature of a gas rises from 10 °C to 20 °C at constant pressure, its volume doubles." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Volume ∝ absolute temperature: 283 K → 293 K increases V by only 3.5 %.
items.markingKey: Volume ∝ absolute temperature: 283 K → 293 K increases V by only 3.5 %. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a real gas and an ideal gas.
items.answer: An ideal gas has particles of zero volume with no intermolecular forces and obeys pV = nRT exactly; a real gas has particles of finite volume with attractions and deviates, especially at high p and low T.
items.markingKey: An ideal gas has particles of zero volume with no intermolecular forces and obeys pV = nRT exactly; a real gas has particles of finite volume with attractions and deviates, especially at high p and low T. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is the temperature of the water bath measured in a Dumas experiment?
options: To check the water is boiling.
To find the density of the vapour.
The vapour temperature is needed in kelvin for pV = nRT.
To calculate the mass of the flask.
items.answer: The vapour temperature is needed in kelvin for pV = nRT.
items.markingKey: C. T is a variable in the equation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Boyle's law and Charles's law.
items.answer: Boyle's law relates p and V at constant T (inverse proportionality); Charles's law relates V and T at constant p (direct proportionality with T in K).
items.markingKey: Boyle's law relates p and V at constant T (inverse proportionality); Charles's law relates V and T at constant p (direct proportionality with T in K). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The value of pV/nRT for a gas at very high pressure is greater than 1. Why?
options: The finite volume of the particles reduces the free space available.
items.answer: The finite volume of the particles reduces the free space available.
items.markingKey: A. Repulsion/particle volume dominates at high p.

items.stem: Explain why a butane lighter should be dried thoroughly before re-weighing in an experiment to find the molar mass of butane collected over water.
items.answer: Water absorbed on the lighter would add to its final mass, making the mass of butane released appear smaller and the calculated molar mass too low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water absorbed on the lighter would add to its final mass, making the mass of butane released appear smaller and the calculated molar mass too low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A 200 cm³ sample of butane in a weather balloon is at 25 °C and 80.0 kPa. Calculate the amount of gas in mol.
1.00 mol of sulfur dioxide at 350 K and 1000 kPa occupies 2.84 dm³. Calculate the volume predicted by the ideal gas equation, the ratio pV/(nRT), and explain the deviation.
items.answer: ideal 2.91 dm³; pV/nRT = 0.975
items.markingKey: V(ideal) = nRT/p = 1.00 × 8.31 × 350/(1000 × 10³) m³ = 2.91 dm³ (M1 A1); pV/nRT = 2.84/2.91 = 0.975 (A1); < 1 because intermolecular attractions (dipole–dipole and London forces) reduce the pressure/volume (R1).

items.stem: A sample of an unknown hydrocarbon was injected into an evacuated bulb. A mass of 0.188 g of the gas occupied 150.0 cm³ at 293 K and 101.3 kPa. Calculate the molar mass of the gas.
items.answer: 30.1 g mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. n = pV/RT (M1); unit conversions to Pa and m³ (M1); M = 30.1 g mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: Noah compresses 30.0 cm³ of air in a syringe at 101 kPa to a pressure of 50 kPa at constant temperature. Calculate the new volume.
items.answer: 60.6 cm³

items.stem: Samples of hydrogen, methane, neon and nitrogen are all at 250 K and 5000 kPa. Which gas behaves most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: D. hydrogen: very weak London forces. Deviation from ideal behaviour increases with the strength of intermolecular forces and the size of the particles.

items.stem: A student claims: "In the gas syringe experiment, the temperature can be used in °C because only a ratio is needed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: pV = nRT requires absolute temperature in kelvin.
items.markingKey: pV = nRT requires absolute temperature in kelvin. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 2.14 mol of chlorine is held in a bulb of volume 0.500 dm³ at 373 K. Calculate the pressure in kPa.

A student released butane gas from a lighter into an inverted measuring cylinder filled with water, collecting 90.0 cm³ of gas. The room temperature was 293 K and atmospheric pressure 100.9 kPa. The vapour pressure of water at 293 K is 2.34 kPa.

mass of lighter before / g ± 0.01 | 20.23
mass of lighter after (dried) / g ± 0.01 | 20.01

(a) Calculate the partial pressure of butane in the cylinder. [1]
(b) Calculate the amount of butane collected. [2]
(c) Determine the experimental molar mass of butane and its percentage error compared with 58.14 g mol⁻¹. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of butane released. [2]
(e) Explain why ignoring the vapour pressure of water would give a lower molar mass (59.0 g mol⁻¹). [1]
items.answer: (a) 98.56 kPa (b) 0.00364 mol (c) 60.4 g mol⁻¹; 3.9 % (d) 9.1 % (e) Using the total pressure overestimates the partial pressure and therefore the amount of butane; M = m/n is then too small.

items.stem: "Determining molar mass from gas measurements is less useful today than mass spectrometry." Discuss.
items.answer: Mass spectrometry is superior for precise identification, but gas-law methods remain valuable for education and quick estimates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: mass spectrometry gives Mr precisely and needs tiny samples; gives structural information too. Arguments against: gas methods are cheap and illustrate the gas laws; useful in teaching labs and field work; accuracy acceptable for identifying simple gases. Supported judgement: Mass spectrometry is superior for precise identification, but gas-law methods remain valuable for education and quick estimates. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "pV = nRT is the only gas equation a chemist needs."
items.answer: It is the central equation but must be applied within its ideal limits and with consistent units.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it combines Boyle, Charles and Avogadro in one equation; works well for most gases at moderate conditions. Arguments against: not valid for real gases at high pressure/low temperature; combined gas law (p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂) is more convenient when n is constant. Supported judgement: It is the central equation but must be applied within its ideal limits and with consistent units. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "The ideal gas model is useful even though no real gas is ideal." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The model is valuable within its domain of validity; for high pressure or low temperature, corrected models (e.g. van der Waals) are required – a NOS example of model limitations.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: accurate within a few percent for most gases near room conditions; simple equation allows quick calculations; basis of molar volume and gas stoichiometry. Arguments against: fails for high-pressure industrial processes (e.g. Haber process at 20 MPa); cannot predict condensation; polar gases deviate significantly. Supported judgement: The model is valuable within its domain of validity; for high pressure or low temperature, corrected models (e.g. van der Waals) are required – a NOS example of model limitations. items.stem: Define the term "Boyle's law".
items.answer: For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, pressure is inversely proportional to volume (pV = constant). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: high temperature and low pressure
items.markingKey: B. Particles far apart and fast: forces and particle volume negligible.

items.stem: When a gas is collected over water, which correction must be made to the measured pressure?
items.answer: subtract the vapour pressure of water at that temperature
items.markingKey: subtract the vapour pressure of water at that temperature. p(gas) = p(atm) − p(H₂O).

items.stem: Explain, using kinetic theory, why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated in a sealed rigid container.
items.answer: Heating increases the average kinetic energy and speed of the particles; they collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure increases (p ∝ T at constant V).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heating increases the average kinetic energy and speed of the particles; they collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure increases (p ∝ T at constant V). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Lars writes: "Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour most at high temperatures because the particles move fastest." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Deviations are greatest at low temperature (and high pressure), when slow particles allow intermolecular attractions to become significant.
items.markingKey: Deviations are greatest at low temperature (and high pressure), when slow particles allow intermolecular attractions to become significant. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: During a gas-syringe determination of the molar mass of a volatile liquid, the atmospheric pressure was taken as 101.3 kPa when it was actually 97.0 kPa. State whether the calculated molar mass will be too high or too low, giving a reason.
items.answer: Too low: p is overestimated; n is too large and M too small.
items.markingKey: too low (1); reasoning via M = mRT/pV: p is overestimated; n is too large and M too small (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "In pV = nRT, volume can be entered in dm³ with pressure in Pa." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Units must be consistent: Pa with m³ (or kPa with dm³); Pa with dm³ gives an answer 1000 times too large.
items.markingKey: Units must be consistent: Pa with m³ (or kPa with dm³); Pa with dm³ gives an answer 1000 times too large. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a gas would liquefy if cooled enough, although an ideal gas never would.
items.answer: Real particles attract each other; at low enough kinetic energy the attractions hold particles together as a liquid; ideal-gas particles have no attractions so cannot condense.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Real particles attract each other; at low enough kinetic energy the attractions hold particles together as a liquid; ideal-gas particles have no attractions so cannot condense. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an experiment to determine the molar mass of a gas using M = mRT/(pV), the atmospheric pressure was taken as 101.3 kPa when it was actually 97.0 kPa. What is the effect on the calculated molar mass?
options: The effect cannot be predicted from the equation.
items.answer: It will be too low.
items.markingKey: D. P is overestimated; n is too large and M too small.

items.stem: A balloon holds 10.0 dm³ of helium at 0 °C. The balloon is moved to a place at 100 °C at the same pressure. What is the new volume?
items.answer: 13.7 dm³
items.markingKey: B. V/T constant: V₂ = 10.0 × 373/273 = 13.7 dm³ (T in K).

items.stem: Under which conditions does hydrogen chloride behave least like an ideal gas?
items.answer: low temperature and high pressure
items.markingKey: D. Low T: attractions significant; high p: particle volume significant compared with the container.

items.stem: A 75.0 cm³ sample of oxygen in a steel cylinder is at 0 °C and 500 kPa. Calculate the amount of gas in mol.
For a sample of carbon dioxide at 273 K and 1000 kPa, the measured value of pV/(nRT) is 1.19. Which statement best explains this value?
options: The particles have a lower kinetic energy than predicted.
The gas behaves ideally under these conditions.
The attractive forces between the particles are significant.
The volume of the particles themselves is significant.
items.answer: The volume of the particles themselves is significant.
items.markingKey: D. pV/nRT = 1 for an ideal gas. Greater than 1: the finite particle volume reduces free space, so the real volume exceeds the ideal volume.

items.stem: A gas syringe was filled with propane. A mass of 0.113 g of the gas occupied 75.0 cm³ at 353 K and 100.0 kPa. Calculate the molar mass of the gas.
items.answer: 44.2 g mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: n = pV/RT (M1); unit conversions to Pa and m³ (M1); M = 44.2 g mol⁻¹ (A1).

items.stem: A car tyre contains air at 200 kPa and 25 °C. After driving, the temperature of the air is 60 °C. Assuming constant volume, calculate the new pressure.
items.answer: 223 kPa
items.markingKey: B. p/T constant (M1); p₂ = 200 × 333/298 = 223 kPa (A1).
